Voyager IQ — Design System

Version 1.2 · 8 November 2026 Linh Long Engineering / Rocket EMS · repository ll-poc Source of truth: src/theme/ · Living specimen: /design-system

Everything in this document was read out of a working build. Every number was taken from the source; every picture was captured from the running application at 2×. Where a figure came from measuring the screen rather than from a rule, it says so.

What changed in 1.2. Four claims in 1.1 were checkable and did not hold up. The route count in C2.3 now says where it comes from. B7 listed three breakpoints where the stylesheets have eleven. E1's contrast row rested on a one-off sweep from 5 September; contrast:check now re-measures 114 token pairs on every push, and found a gap in the light theme the same day — subtle is a measured value now, see B1.3. And progress was the one status nobody had darkened, so a dark grid showed one bright cyan chip among seven dark ones (B1.6). 1.2 also says what this file does not cover yet. A1 states the scope — foundations complete, and all 29 component pages written as of 8 Nov — and F4 lists the gaps against what the published systems do, rechecked against those systems rather than against blogs about them. What changed in 1.1. The type scale printed in 1.0 was the @media (pointer: coarse) block, not the default — six values, all in B2, published two sizes too large. Corrected against tokens.css. B2 also still described a second font family; mono was dropped for identifiers on 13 October at the customer's request, finished on 22 October, and the token and the webfont were removed on 7 November. The one step still below the 12px floor, --vy-text-2xs at 10px, was raised. Nothing else in the document moved: the other 156 token values were already exact.

Part A — Start here

A1 · What this is

The file someone needs to build a new Voyager IQ screen without asking, and the file a reviewer needs to tell a correct screen from a plausible one.

It is not a style guide for a drawing tool. It describes a system that is running: the tokens are CSS custom properties, the components are React, and the specimen page renders the real thing.

How far that goes today, stated rather than implied. The foundations — Part B — are complete: every token in src/theme/ is here at its measured value, and six checks re-prove them on every push. The components are not. Part D covers four families — buttons, fields, grids, dialogs — out of the 29 components in src/ui, and covers them as prose rather than as the specification a reference system gives each component: when to use it, when not to, its anatomy, its variants against its states, and a do and a don't. One component, Button, has a live specimen. So: this file is enough to get the colour, type, spacing, density and behaviour of a new screen right, and enough to review one. It is not yet enough to pick the right control without reading src/ui. What is missing and in what order it should be filled is in F4.

A2 · The three layers

LayerWhat it isWhereMay a screen use it?
1 · RampsThe raw palette. 10 blues, 12 greys, 4 redstokens.cssNo
2 · Semantic rolessurface, on-surface, brand, danger… named for the jobtokens.cssYes — only this
3 · ComponentsButton, Field, Grid, Dialog…src/ui, src/componentsYes

A stylesheet saying background: var(--vy-grey-0) has hard-coded white, and no theme can move it. One saying var(--vy-surface) has hard-coded "the colour a panel is", which a theme is allowed to answer differently.

Layer 1 exists so that layer 2 can be consistent. It is not for use in a component.

A3 · Five rules before you build

  1. Is there a token? If yes, use it. If no, add one — and say in the code why the scale did not already have it.
  2. Do not invent content. Field names, option lists, status words and behaviour are facts about the business, not design decisions. Look them up before drawing them.
  3. Both themes, both densities, 820px. A screen that has only been seen in light mode on a 1920px monitor has been seen once.
  4. A magic number carries a note. A width that deviates from its role needs a widthNote saying what was measured.
  5. Say what is not real. A derived figure, an unbuilt action and a fake send are each labelled where they appear, not only in a commit message.

B1.3 Text colour — six tiers

on-surface is body copy; strong sits above it for headings and identifiers.

A tier is set by its worst ground, not by the panel. subtle is the second value in the system chosen by measurement rather than taken from the ramp — after --vy-border-control, and for the same reason: no step conforms. grey-500 #626d7e clears 4.5 on white, the page and the sunken panel but reaches only 4.02 on surface-strong; grey-600 overshoots to 5.62, where it stops being distinguishable from muted and the tier stops being a tier. #5b6575 sits on grey-500's own hue one notch darker and clears every ground, the tightest being surface-strong at 4.53.

⚠️ on-surface-faint measures 2.58:1 on white. Legitimate only on a dark ground or where the text is decorative — never for anything a user has to read. It is the one declared exemption in contrast:check; everything else in the table is checked on every push.

B1.4 Lines

border is structure — panel edges, table rules — which WCAG 1.4.11 does not cover. border-control is the boundary of something you can operate, which it does cover.

It is one of two values in the system chosen by measurement rather than by the ramp — the other is on-surface-subtle. The sweep of 5 September found why: the grey ramp has no step that conforms. grey-400 #97a2b2 is 2.58:1 against white and misses by 0.42; the next step overshoots to 5.24, where it would be indistinguishable from the text it sits beside. A value was introduced between them. It governs boundaries only: input, textarea, combobox, checkbox, radio, and anything else whose edge is its shape — a chip, an outlined button, a colour swatch.

"The lightest value that conforms" conformed against one ground, and that took until 8 November to notice. The September value, #8a94a6, was measured on white. A control also sits on the page, in a sunken strip, on a hover tint, on a selected row. Swept across every ground on 8 Nov it cleared exactly one of them: | surface | subtle | app | hover | selected | sunken | strong | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | 3.06 | 2.98 | 2.85 | 2.85 | 2.78 | 2.65 | 2.35 | Which is how a checkbox measured 2.85 in the control sweep while the Kendo bridge was already pointing it at this token: the token was right and the value was short. A boundary is set by its worst ground, the same rule as a text tier. #758096 is the lightest value on the same hue and saturation line that clears 3 on all of them, tightest at 3.05 on surface-strong. contrast:check now measures every boundary against every ground rather than against the panel, so this cannot come back.
And then the same mistake, one state along — 9 November. 1.4.11 covers a control's states, and both checks were resting-state only: one reads the palette, the other sweeps a page nobody is pointing at. .vy-input:hover and .vy-sup-btn:hover drew their edge with --vy-border-heavy, and the comment beside the rule explains itself in light mode alone — "grey-500, not grey-400; the resting border is now darker than grey-400, so the old hover was lighter than the state it was meant to emphasise." True on white. In dark the resting border is #707c8d and grey-500 is darker than it, so one declaration made the hover both fainter than the resting state and non-conforming: measured in the running build at 2.68 on the panel, 2.41 on a raised one, 2.02 on surface-strong. One value cannot do it, for the reason B1.5 already gives about fill and text: more visible is darker on white and lighter on near-black. So the hover boundary is a role of its own. Light takes grey-500 from the ramp — 5.24 on a panel against the resting 3.97, so nothing changes in light. Dark has no step that works: grey-500 and border-mid are darker than the resting border, and grey-400 is lighter than on-surface-subtle, which would leave a hovered edge outshining the quietest text on the page. #858f9e is one notch up border-control's own hue and saturation line — 5.23 on a panel, 3.95 on surface-strong, within 0.07 of what light gets. Both themes now land a hovered boundary at about 4:1 on their worst ground. Measured on .vy-input, both themes, with transitions stopped: | | rest | hover, was | hover, now | focus, was | focus, now | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | light | 3.97 | 5.24 | 5.24 | 4.48 | 6.82 | | dark | 4.04 | 2.68 | 5.23 | 3.82 | 9.58 | border:check now sweeps three states, so the next one is not found by hand. The full list, and the three attribute-borne states it still cannot reach, is in vien-state-09nov.md.

B1.5 Brand and danger

Fill and text are separate roles, because in a dark theme they pull opposite ways: a fill must be dark enough for its label, brand text light enough for the page. The dark theme inverts the pair rather than shifting it.

So do the boundaries, and one of them was left behind. boundary-strong means one step more emphatic than boundary — darker in light, lighter in dark. It is the focus edge of every text input, the rich-text surface and every editable cell. When the focus ring moved off blue-400 on 8 Nov for measuring 2.88 on surface-strong, the edge kept it: in dark, "strong" was darker than plain boundary, and therefore weaker than it. Both tokens had been measured in the same pass and only one moved. blue-200 restores the relationship — tightest 7.22 — and 9 Nov.

boundary-soft and boundary-light stay below 3:1 on purpose: they draw banner edges, the verdict panel and a horizontal rule, which 1.4.11 does not cover. Two controls were pointing at them anyway, and the state pass found both.

B1.6 Status vocabulary

Eight statuses, each a foreground/background pair.

A status is a word and a colour, never a colour alone. The pair is what makes it legible to someone who cannot separate the hues.

The dark pairs are constructed, not picked: the foreground runs between 96 and ee, the background between 1e and 38, and the middle channel carries the hue. Every pair lands between 6.16:1 and 9.30:1.

progress only joined them on 8 November. Seven statuses inverted for dark and that one kept its light pair, so a dark grid showed a single bright cyan chip among seven dark ones. Worth knowing because it is still the closest pair in the vocabulary: progress and review are 1.5° apart in hue in light and 6° in dark, and the word is what separates them. If the two are ever confused on screen the answer is a different hue for one of them, not a darker cyan.

A fill that carries no text takes the -fg half, not the -bg one. The Home chart draws each series from this vocabulary, and a segment is not a chip: -bg is pale by design, because text sits on it. Measured on 9 November, the In-Progress series read --vy-status-progress-bg and came to 1.12:1 against the light card and 1.37:1 against the dark one. The five chart fills are now in contrast:check for exactly that reason — nothing had ever measured a shape with no text on it. --vy-chart-cancelled is the one chart-only value. As badges, New and Cancelled sit on separate rows and a near-identical grey costs nothing; in a stacked bar they touch, and the badge greys are 1.35:1 apart in light and identical in dark. The badge tokens are the customer's specification and stay as they are. See Dashboard.

B1.7 Row tones and accents

A tone is a row's state in the quote, not a severity. Three of them paint most of a BoM grid, and the legend under the grid names all three.

Amber does three jobs, and that is allowed because of two rules. The same #fef3c7 is the open status, the short row tone and the known-mfg row tone. The objection writes itself — yellow should mean warning and nothing else — so here is the measured answer rather than an assertion:

  1. They never meet. short paints the Quoting and Quote Result grids, known-mfg paints Review BoM, and neither of those grids has a status column — checked, not assumed: zero columns with role: 'status' in either. An amber pill and an amber row cannot appear on one screen.
  2. Every amber grid carries a legend that names what its amber means, on that screen. A colour only the author can decode is a colour that means nothing; a colour with a key beside it is a colour with one meaning.

What amber consistently means across all three is needs attention, nothing is broken — which is why blocked and missing are red and not a darker amber.

Which of the two ambers. --vy-accent-warning #b45309 is the default and has twelve call sites; --vy-accent-caution #d97706 has one, the email-mode composer border. They are 17.9 ΔE apart, so they are genuinely distinguishable — this is not a duplicate pair — but the system never said which to reach for, and twice a comment in the code had to decide it in passing. Stated now: warning for anything the user should act on, caution only where two amber levels appear together and the lower one needs to recede. One place does that today. A second token with one call site and no rule is how a palette drifts.

B1.8 How dark mode is wired

Three blocks, and a token must appear in all three or the two ways of choosing dark disagree:

BlockWho it serves
:root { … }Light — the default
:root[data-theme="dark"] { … }A user who picked dark in the user menu
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { … } }A user whose OS is dark
This has already failed once: four tokens existed only in the media copy, so a user who picked dark in the menu got grey-400 borders and a near-white priority dot on a near-black ground. Adding a colour token means editing three places.

The same two blocks in the dark theme. Every role keeps its job and changes its value — and the status pairs stay legible rather than being inverted mechanically:

B2 · Typography

One family. Inter Variable, everywhere, self-hosted — no request to Google and no flash of fallback text.

There was a second. JetBrains Mono set the identifiers: part numbers, MPNs, RFQ and assembly numbers. The review of 13 October ended it — "do not use monotext, hard to read" — .vy-ident was rewritten the same day, and the last holdout, the MiniTable grids in Run Quotation, went on 22 October. On 22 October the customer also said what mono had been for: a unique value should not look like an ordinary field. So the requirement is prominence, not a typeface — and prominence is cheaper than a second font. An identifier is semibold, in the strong ink, with tabular-nums, which is what held the digits in columns all along. A part number is read as a word by people who know their catalogue; at 12–13px in a dense grid the mono face was the thing slowing them down. The token and the webfont were removed on 7 November.

Five weights, and the top three are finely spaced on purpose — measured. "650 and 700 are too close to 600" is the obvious objection, so it was measured rather than argued: the same string rendered at 13px in Inter Variable, by width and by ink coverage.

400500600650700
width234.30237.03239.76241.12242.48
ink111k128k146k154k162k
step—+15.7%+13.4%+5.6%+5.5%

They are all distinct — Inter Variable spans 100–900, nothing snaps — but the top two steps are about a third of the steps below them. So the honest rule is not "five interchangeable weights":

WeightJobCall sites
regular 400Body text22
medium 500A label, a button, a link that must hold its line59
semibold 600The default emphasis. Identifiers, group headings, totals112
bold 650A page or record title, where 600 is already in use nearby42
heavy 700A number that is the whole point of its tile — a KPI, a queue count12

Reach for 600. Use 650 and 700 only where something at 600 is next to them and has to stay quieter; at a 5% step they do not read as emphasis on their own.

12px is the floor, agreed with the customer on 22 October. It was 11px; our own small-text check had flagged anything under 12 all along. The floor collapses the bottom of the scale — 2xs, xs and sm all sit on it, three names carrying one size. The names stay because they mean different things: a badge, a label, secondary text.

A finger un-collapses it. Under @media (pointer: coarse) the bottom three come apart again — 12, 13, 14 — and every step above them moves +2, to 15, 16 and 18. Display sizes (xl and up) do not move: they are already comfortable, and growing a heading on a 375px screen buys nothing and costs a wrap. The floor is never crossed in either direction.

Casing — three levels, drawn differently on purpose

Buttons, links, tabs, form and dialog titles, section and card titles, field labels, column headers, filter labels, menu items and status pills take Title Case, with prepositions (for, to, of, by, as, in, on, at, from, with, via, per, into) lowercase unless they lead. Prose is sentence case.

LevelCaseSize / weightExample
Card headerTitle Case14px / 600Select Action · Continue from Drafts
Divider inside a cardUPPERCASE, .05em tracking12px / 600QUOTE STRATEGY · BOM OPTIONS
Field labelTitle Case12px / 600Customer · Qty to Quote · Markup (%)

B3.2 Which gap goes between two controls

The scale does not say which step to pick, so the system states it. The tiers are what carry grouping, which is why they are not collapsed into one value:

GapBetweenExamples
2pxButtons in a cluster that reads as one controldialog titlebar, pager arrows
4pxIcon buttons attached to the control they act ona Select with Preview and Download
8pxTwo adjacent actions — the default.vy-page-actions, .vy-run-nav-actions, .vy-cost-actions
12pxItems that each hold a control and a labelfilter checkboxes, which are 8px from their own words
16pxGroups on one rowtoolbar filters / search / Columns

Two buttons side by side are 8px apart everywhere. A bigger gap means a real boundary, not a different author.

B4 · Shape, elevation, depth

Four radii, three shadows. Elevation is for things that float — a dialog, a menu, a toast. A card on a page gets a border, not a shadow.

Every control sits on Kendo's own size scale, configured rather than overridden — _kendo-size.scss sets the variables and the components inherit them. Forcing a height on a Kendo control instead is how a 29px select ends up beside a 34px input.

B6 · Motion

Four easings and three durations, and nothing else. There is deliberately no loop-length token: a custom property nothing reads is a token that rots.

TokenValueUse
--vy-ease-standardcubic-bezier(.2, 0, 0, 1)The default. Everything, unless it has a reason

The loading clock

RuleValue
Show the boot screen only if the boot takes longer than400ms
Exit — the craft leaves the top of the frame400ms
"Still climbing…" appears after5s
Minimum display time once shownnone

Holding a loading screen so it does not flash spends the user's time to make our indicator look better. Not showing one at all for a boot that beats the clock costs them nothing. The two rules are the two halves of one answer.

Reduced motion is a state, not a switch

Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce the rocket holds its pose — no climb, no flicker, no streaks — and the step bar still fills. A welding arm with its animation removed is an arm with no sparks and an empty checklist, which says something different from what the state means, so the things that fade in are left on.

B7 · Responsive

Breakpoints are raw pixels because @media cannot read custom properties — a documented exception to the no-magic-numbers rule.

Three of them are the shell, in responsive.css, and they are the ones worth knowing by heart:

WidthWhat changes
≤ 1180pxThe 248px sidebar becomes a 56px icon rail
≤ 980pxTwo-column regions stack
≤ 820pxThe sidebar leaves the flow; a menu button reveals it
pointer: coarseThe bottom of the type scale re-expands; 44px target floor

Eight more are component breakpoints, and the honest count is eleven, not three. A component that needs one measures it and carries the measurement — rule 4 of A3 — rather than being bent to fit a shell width it has nothing to do with:

WidthWhereWhat it answers
≤ 1100pxtop bar, tab stripThe timezone picker goes; the clock still states the zone
≤ 900pxtop bar, cost summary, submit barThe clock goes; a 2fr/1fr money split stacks before its figures stop lining up
≤ 860pxrecord header
≤ 840pxwizard stepperFour labelled steps need ~760px; below it they truncate, and a truncated step name is worse than none
≤ 720pxpage bodyA real phone, or a genuinely short window
≤ 700pxstepper, link columnsOnly the current step keeps its label; the others become their marker, still positioned and still clickable
≤ 620pxrecord header
≤ 560pxfilter stripA right-anchored strip would read as clipped at this width

Two of those — 860 and 620 — carry no note, which rule 4 says they should.

The system runs on shop-floor terminals that are often 1366×768 or narrower. Below about 1100px a 248px sidebar stops being orientation and starts being the thing in the way — measured at 543px it was taking 46% of the viewport.

The same screen at the three widths that matter. Full rail, icon rail, and no rail at all with a menu button in the top bar — and in all three the grid keeps its columns rather than shrinking them:

B8 · Layout

A page in this app is three things across: the sidebar, two gutters and the content box. B7 says when the sidebar changes size; this section says what the content box does about it, and what it is allowed to grow to.

Written on 9 November 2026, and it is the last structural section the system was missing. Everything below was measured rather than decided: grid:check sweeps 6 routes × 12 widths and the numbers in this section are its output.

B8.1 What takes the width before the content does

Measured as an identity rather than a formula, so moving a breakpoint cannot make this wrong:

rail + gutters + content = viewport. Nothing else may take a share.
ViewportRailGuttersContent
≤ 820px0 — the sidebar is fixed and off-screen2 × 14vw − 28
821–1180px56 — icon rail2 × 14vw − 84
≥ 1181px248 — labelled2 × 24vw − 296, up to the cap

The content box, measured on each page shape:

vw375600768820900980110011801280136614401920
list34757274079281689610161096984107011441624
everything else34757274079281689610161096984107011321132

B8.2 The step at 1180 is negative, and it is the only one

Read the row again at the two widths either side of it.

At 1180px the content box is 1096px. At 1280px it is 984px. The window gained 100px and the page lost 112.

Crossing 1180 upward the rail goes 56 → 248 and the gutters 14 → 24: 212px taken, 100px given. The consequence is not theoretical — a 1366 laptop, the machine this product is mostly used on, shows 1070px of content where an 1180 terminal shows 1096px.

It is a trade, not a bug. The labelled rail is orientation, which is what decision D1 bought and what the 25 August review asked for; the alternative is an icon rail on every laptop in the building. And the user has an escape worth 192px — the collapse control, which is only offered above 1180 because below it the rail is already collapsed.

The breakpoint that would remove the step entirely is 1392px, not 1180: content above it is vw − 296, so the window has to reach 1392 before the expanded rail pays for itself. Moving it there would deny the labelled rail to every 1366 screen, which is the wrong half of the trade.

What the system does instead is declare the step, and grid:check fails if a second one appears anywhere.

B8.3 Four page shapes, and until 9 November only two had a width

ShapeUsed byCap
.vy-page--gridEvery list screennone, on purpose
.vy-page--recordThe RFQ record--vy-record-max-w
.vy-page--docDesign system, Audit, Sitemap--vy-doc-max-w
.vy-pageHome, My Queues, Placeholderwas none — now --vy-page-max

All three caps are the same number, 1180px, and the two named tokens now resolve to --vy-page-max so there is one value rather than three that happen to agree.

The list shape is uncapped, and that has to stay a decision. The widest grid in this product is 1806px at its default view — Project Requirements, 12 columns at their B5.3 role widths — and 2106px with every column turned on, which is Part Master at 16. Any cap below those would create horizontal scrolling on a window that had the width to avoid it. The role widths themselves hold at every width: measured at 2560px the table is still 1806px and every column is still its declared width, so a 2560 screen shows the whole grid with the remainder of the frame empty.

Everything else is capped, and the base rule is what carries it — so a page that declares nothing now gets the conservative width rather than the unbounded one. That inversion is the point: before, the default was infinite.

The cost of not capping was measurable on the two dashboard screens:

At a 1920 viewportUncappedCapped
Chart column127px, holding a 28px bar — 99px of air between bars85px, 57px of air
Queue tile397px for a one-digit number and two short lines274px

A page with no grid to fill has nothing to spend the width on, and twelve bars spread across 1600px stop reading as a series.

Left-aligned, not centred. A list screen is full-bleed, so a centred dashboard would make the page title jump right as you navigate from a grid to Home. The heading starts at the same x on every screen; the unused width is left where it is.

B8.4 Columns — one idiom, sixteen minimums

There is no 12-column grid here, and that is deliberate. A fixed column count assumes the content box has a stable width; this one changes by 640px across the range above, loses 112px at one step, and is capped on four shapes out of five. Sixteen layout grids, all of them the same idiom:

grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(var(--some-min), 1fr));

The tracks are equal, they consume the row at any count and any width, and the floor is what decides when a row wraps. So the only number a layout grid chooses is the width below which its content stops being readable — and that is a property of the content, not of the grid. A count tile and a form field group do not stop being readable at the same width, so they do not share a number.

GridMinimum tokenMinimumColumn gapWhat it holds
.vy-kpi-row--vy-kpi-min-w140px8pxCount tiles over a list
.vy-bom-summary--vy-stat-min-w150px10pxFigures over a BoM
.vy-run-ref .vy-quote-config-grid--vy-quote-ref-field-min150pxinheritedReference fields, narrow pane
.vy-stat-row--vy-stat-min-w150px10pxFigures in a summary strip
.vy-assy-grid--vy-assy-field-min170pxinheritedAssembly fields
.vy-contact-fields--vy-contact-field-min180px10pxContact fields
.vy-filter-fields--vy-filter-field-min190px12pxFilter fields
.vy-quote-context-fields--vy-quote-fact-w190px10pxQuote context facts
.vy-record-fields--vy-header-field-min190px16pxRecord-header facts
.vy-assignees--vy-card-min-w200pxinheritedAssignee cards, stacked
.vy-queue-row--vy-card-min-w200px12pxQueue cards
.vy-radios--tiles--vy-radio-tile-min230px10pxRadio tiles
.vy-quote-config-grid--vy-quote-field-min240px16pxQuote configuration fields
.vy-header-groups--vy-header-group-min260px12pxRecord-header groups
.vy-field-groups--vy-field-group-min280px20pxForm field groups
.vy-notes-edit--vy-note-min-w320px16pxNote editors, side by side

Eleven distinct minimums and six distinct gaps, and the system does not flatten them onto a ladder. It states the catalogue instead: a new grid picks a row from it, or measures its own and records why — A3 rule 4, the same rule B7 applies to breakpoints. What grid:check enforces is that the minimum is a token, so a seventeenth value cannot arrive as a literal in a rule.

B8.5 What grid:check measures

node scripts/with-server.mjs grid:check · 72 measurements, 6 routes × 12 widths, in check:visual on every push.

The identityrail + gutters + content = viewport, at every width. Nothing else may take a share
The capsA capped shape never exceeds --vy-page-max
The opt-outThe list shape is still uncapped at the widest width swept — so the decision in B8.3 cannot decay into an omission
One stepContent width never falls as the viewport grows, except between 1180 and 1280
TokensEvery auto-fit minimum is a var(), never a literal

Two faults are planted on every run — a cap forced onto the list shape, and a literal minimum — and the run fails if either goes unseen.

What it deliberately does not check is horizontal page overflow. mobile:check owns that, along with its 198 open tablet findings; duplicating them here would make this check red for a reason that has nothing to do with the grid.

C1 · Icons

One set. 20×20 viewBox, stroke only, no fill, one stroke weight. A heavier line at a smaller size is how an icon set stops looking like one set.

An unknown name renders nothing, with the name left in the DOM, rather than falling back to a document glyph that hides the bug.

Default size16px · --vy-icon-sm

The 45 names: task · chat · log · quote · order · return · customer · requisition · supplier · factory · simulate · bom · transfer · adjust · pcb · tool · machine · invoice · journal · lock · people · template · job · plug · menu · globe · metadata · queue · doc · home · sell · buy · parts · stock · make · finance · insight · settings · chevron-down · chevron-right · eye · download · clip · trash · check

Two directional glyphs, each with one job: down opens a menu below itself, right says "this opens somewhere else".

C2 · Illustrations

One drawing, three states. The product has exactly one illustrated character — a rocket — and it appears in three situations. That is deliberate: a reader who has met this craft on the way in should not have to learn a second picture to understand that it crashed.

Component: src/ui/RocketLaunch.tsx · one inline SVG, viewBox="0 0 240 180" · data-state selects the scene.

C2.1 launching — the boot screen

The craft holds still in the middle of the frame and the world moves: the planet sinks a notch per boot stage, streaks run down past it. Nothing about a rocket drawn nose-up says "climbing" on its own.

Shown with its label and five-segment bar, which is what the boot screen actually is:

The same craft, back on the pad: tilted, cracked, one fin lying beside it, smoking. The failure is legible before the sentence under it is read.

The craft whole on the pad, a robot arm welding it, a design doc on an easel whose checklist ticks off. Work in progress, not wreckage — and the difference has to be visible before the heading is read.

A skeleton answers "what will this look like?". Once the user has already seen rows that question is answered, so a re-price or a second page dims what is there and puts an indicator over it instead (BusyOverlay).

Part D — Components and patterns

src/ui holds 33 files: the primitives, plus the icon set, the preference store and three hooks. Each wrapper has a reason, and the rule that produced them is the same every time — the live system already ships KendoReact, so the question is never "what should this look like" but "what does Kendo already do, and what must we add".

Component pages

Each one is a full specification — when to use and when not to, anatomy, variants and states, content, behaviour, accessibility, API, and its own change log. All 29. button.md is the model; the rest of Part D below is the older, thinner prose it replaces.

Each page was written against the running build, and each one found something — a wrong contrast ratio, a missing ARIA attribute, a comment describing a rule that was not there. That was the argument for writing all 29, and it held to the last page: people-picker.md turned up a dashed boundary at 1.64:1 that border:check cannot reach, because the control only renders once a record is in edit mode. Writing field.md's hover row the next day turned up the other half of it: the states no sweep was looking at, including the hover edge of that same input at 2.02:1 in dark and the focus edge of every input in the product. Both checks now measure states, which is the part worth keeping — see vien-state-09nov.md.

D1 · Buttons

The full page is components/button.md — when to use and when not to, anatomy, every variant and state, content, keyboard behaviour, accessibility and the API. It is the model page: the shape every other component should be written in, and the reason the rest of Part D reads thin by comparison. What follows here is the summary.

The picture above is the live specimen with the keyboard on it: Text carries the focus ring every control in the system uses — 2px of --vy-brand-boundary offset by 2px, never a removed outline.

VariantWhen
filledOne per view. The most likely next step
outlinedThe default for everything else
tonalA secondary action that still needs weight
textTertiary, inside dense rows
dangerDestructive — and it goes behind More ▾

Placement: all buttons on the left of a toolbar; a smart-button group or step indicator on the right; at most four visible, the rest behind More ▾ — and the label is always the word More with a chevron, never ⋯.

Cancel only in dialogs. In edit mode the word is Discard Changes.

busy is not decoration. The indicator says something is happening; the disable is what stops a second click spending a second marketplace request.

D2 · Fields

Two modes, three presentations

A record has two modes — view and edit. Inside edit mode a field is one of two kinds, and that is what the padlock is for. It is not a third state of a field; it is the mark that separates the two kinds, and it exists only where the distinction is live.

Field the user can changeField the user cannot
View modeSunken box, no padlockSunken box, no padlock
Edit modeWhite input, --vy-border-controlSunken box, padlock, and a short reason

In view mode nothing is editable, so the distinction has nothing to say — a padlock on all twenty-seven fields marks none of them. The boxes are identical and the eye reads the values, not the chrome.

In edit mode the white tells you where you may type. Everything still in a grey box is a value this screen does not own, and the padlock is followed by the reason in two or three words, because a padlock says that a field is locked and cannot say why.

View mode — one box for every value:

Edit mode — white where you may type; grey, padlocked and explained where you may not. Created Date reads set by the system; ITAR reads follows Customer:

One exception, and it is the same rule. A panel where nothing is editable keeps the grey box and drops the padlock — Run Quotation's setup strip on the last step, where the run is finished. A padlock on each of seven values says only what the panel already says.

The rest of a field

PartRule
LabelAbove the value, never beside it. Title Case, 12px, 600
RequiredA red asterisk right after the label, in view and edit mode
OptionalNo mark. Never the word "(optional)"
HelperBelow the field, italic, at or below the label's size
ErrorRed text below the field, on blur — not on every keystroke
Error or hintNever both: two lines, each claiming to say what to do next
HintA sibling of the label, never inside it, or it joins the accessible name

D3 · Grids

A grid is where this system does most of its work, and the row tone is how it talks. A tone is a row's state in the quote, not a severity: green is covered by the chosen supplier, amber is short of the quantity, red is no bid, grey is excluded from the quote entirely.

Every tone is named under the grid it paints. A colour that only the author can decode is a colour that means nothing:

Rule
Column chooserOn every grid with 3+ columns
Frozen blockDeclared as locked, so the chooser and the freeze cannot disagree
ZebraBy record, not by row — a record spanning two AML rows is one band
TotalsA grid the user sums by eye gets a totals row
EmptyA real empty state that says what to do, never "No records available"
WidthBy role (B5.3); a deviation carries a widthNote

D4 · Dialogs

Sizes are in B5.4. Three further rules:

  1. Actions top-left on a work surface, in a footer on a question. The way out goes on the left wherever the bar sits.
  2. lg and xl open maximised; md never does. Those two are the work surfaces, and a 21-column grid in a 1180px window spends the screen it was given — while a confirmation filling a 27-inch screen is a worse answer than the one it replaced.
  3. Escape dismisses the innermost thing, which the Select had to be taught by hand — Kendo's own handling closed the dialog from an open dropdown.

D5 · The four screen states

Loading, empty, error and not-yet-built are four different things and look it. Getting these wrong is the most common way a screen lies to its reader.

StateWhat the user seesActionsIllustration
LoadingRocket climbing, planet sinking, five-segment barnoneC2.1
EmptyA sentence saying what would fill itthe action that fills itnone
ErrorRocket on the pad: tilted, cracked, one fin off, smokingReload · Back to Home · Send a support ticket · Error ID + CopyC2.2
Under developmentRocket whole on the pad, arm welding, plan ticking offBack to Home. No Reload — nothing is brokenC2.3

The error state's three slots are the three questions a person actually has: what failed · what it means for me · what I can do next. Only the first is generic.

The error id is minted where the error is caught, not where it is drawn — minted in render, pressing Copy would hand the user a different number for the same failure.

D6 · Words

CasingB2 — Title Case for labels, sentence case for prose
A control says what happensPublish, then a toast saying Published
An error says what to doNot "Something went wrong"
Nothing is "not implemented" silentlyA toast says what it would do
A derived figure says it is derived"Derived from this run — the live system takes them from the customer's purchase history"
A session-only change says so"Added in this session… nothing here is saved"

Two measurements, and they answer different questions. contrast-sweep.md of 5 September is the real one: a browser, a canvas pixel per element, backgrounds composited up the ancestor chain, because Kendo emits oklch() and no regex over getComputedStyle survives it. That sweep is what found the three control borders. It is also a one-off — it ran once, against the palette of that day, and the dark theme, the status vocabulary and the 12px floor all landed afterwards.

contrast:check is the cheap half, kept honest about being the cheap half. It reads tokens.css, resolves every var() chain in both themes, and checks the pairs the system promises: each text tier on each ground it can sit on, brand and danger, all eight status pills, the row tones, and the two non-text boundaries. No browser, no server. It cannot see a component that puts text on a ground the system never intended, or an opacity that makes the real ground something no token states — those still need the browser sweep. What it does catch is the palette drifting out from under this document, which is what happened between September and November, and it caught one the day it was written: subtle on surface-strong at 4.02:1. See B1.3.

Why the harness can be trusted. Colours in the September sweep are read through a canvas pixel rather than parsed from strings. Before the results were believed, a #bbbbbb-on-white element was planted in the page and caught at 1.92:1. contrast:check plants the same value on every run and exits non-zero if it fails to detect it — a sweep that reports no failures is only worth reading if it can prove it would have found one.

Four rules that are easy to get wrong and are already settled:

  • A status is a word and a colour, never a colour alone.
  • A hint is a sibling of the label, never inside it.
  • role="alert" for an error, role="status" for a loading state. One interrupts, the other does not.
  • A decorative glyph is aria-hidden and the state it marks gets words of its own — a padlock plus a screen-reader-only "read-only".

E2 · KendoReact

The live system already ships KendoReact 16. The bridge is three files:

FileJob
kendo-subset.scssCompiles only the Kendo components actually used
_kendo-size.scssConfigures Kendo's size scale — does not override it
kendo-bridge.cssMaps Kendo's variables onto ours, and fixes what cannot be configured

Specificity is the trap. .k-button.k-button-solid.k-button-base.k-focus weighs (0,4,0), so a one-class rule of ours loses silently. The bridge prefixes with html[data-kendo-bridged] rather than repeating a class five times.

Two Kendo behaviours worth knowing before debugging a component:

  • Kendo disables with a .k-disabled CLASS, not the :disabled attribute. A plain <input disabled class="k-radio"> renders identically to an enabled one.
  • KendoReact 16 locks grid columns with sticky cells in one table (position: sticky), not with two panes.

F2 · How to change something

A colour token

  1. Add or change it in all three blocks of tokens.css (B1.8).
  2. If it lands on text or a control boundary, re-run the contrast sweep.
  3. npm run check:fast — lint, stylesheet check, typecheck, build.

A component

  1. Check whether Kendo already does it (E2).
  2. Build it in src/ui, referencing semantic tokens only.
  3. Add a specimen to /design-system if it has states worth seeing.
  4. Cover every state: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, busy, error.

A new screen

  1. Which of the four states (D5) can it be in? Build all of them.
  2. Column roles, not pixel widths.
  3. Check it at 1180, 980 and 820, in both themes.

What CI runs on every push: contrast:check (inside css:check, so it gates the build) · render:check · touch:check · mobile:check · focus:check · hover:check · border:check.

F3 · Governance

Source of truthsrc/theme/ and the components in src/ui. This file describes them; it does not define them
Where a decision is recordedIn the code, at the rule it governs — and in a dated note under docs/ when a reader would otherwise have to re-derive it
JudgementAllowed where nothing else answers, and labelled as judgement where it is used
Versioningv1.0 is this handover. A token or rule change is a minor version; a change that requires screens to be rebuilt is a major one

Three rules that keep this document true:

  1. A magic number needs a note saying what was measured.
  2. A comment states what was measured, not what was intended. Three corrections in this project came from a comment describing behaviour the code did not have.
  3. The living page beats the document. /design-system renders the real components; if the two disagree, the page is right and this file is stale.

F4 · What a handover should contain

The shape of this document was checked against current practice rather than invented. The November check was redone against the published systems themselves rather than against blogs about them, and it changed the answer: the earlier version of this section listed what a handover should contain and did not say which of it this file actually has. Both columns are below.

What the published systems doHere
Tokens with their values, in named tiersA2, B1–B6. Three tiers — ramp, role, component — the same model as Material 3's palette → role → component, and compatible with the W3C token format
Accessibility with the thresholds namedE1, and measured per token pair rather than asserted. Carbon names the same thresholds but publishes no per-token values; GOV.UK names them inside one component
Responsive with the breakpoints statedB7 — all eleven, shell and component, since 1.2
Motion with duration, easing, reduced-motionB6
Governance — ownership, contribution, versioningF2, F3
Component specs: when to use · when not to · anatomy · variants × states · content · behaviour · accessibility · code · do and don'tAll 29, in docs/components/, to that shape. D1–D4 remain as the older, thinner prose
Patterns — form, filter, destructive action, notification, page templateEight, in docs/patterns/
A lifecycle status per component — trial · stable · deprecatedOn every page, GOV.UK's three. Four are trial, each for a stated reason: file drop, rich text, support ticket, chip
A changelog per componentOn every page, as a Recent changes table with dates. F3 still holds the versioning policy
Layout grid as a foundationB8 — the container ladder, the one idiom and its sixteen minimums, measured by grid:check

Nothing on the checklist is left, as of 9 November. docs/chuan-design-system.md carries the comparison in full, the component template these 29 pages were written against, and the triage that ordered them.

The layout grid was last on the list on the argument that it is the least useful of the three until the screens stop changing shape. Writing it found the opposite: two of the four page shapes had no declared width at all, and the content box loses 112px at one breakpoint while the window gains 100. Both had been true since the shell was built, and neither was visible without measuring every width.

Every source also names the one failure mode this file is most exposed to: documentation drifting away from the live code once the team moves on. That is why F3 makes the specimen page the tie-breaker rather than this document, and why the numbers above are re-proved by contrast:check rather than restated.

Read directly, 8 November 2026: Carbon — Button usage · Carbon — Accessibility: colour · Atlassian — Foundations · Atlassian — Button · GOV.UK — Button · GOV.UK — Component lifecycle statuses · W3C Design Tokens format (draft) · Material 3 — Colour roles. The W3C format is a draft that says not to implement it yet; the rest are each one organisation's practice, not a standard. They agree on the shape and differ on depth.
